events.text: Day 1 begins.

Day 1, and none of us have anything concrete yet — no night deaths reported, no role information, so any read right now is gut work. I'll say where I stand so people can test it: my instinct puts Felix at the top of my suspicion list, but only as a talking order, not a conviction. Villagers with no night kill this early usually give themselves away by how they steer the vote rather than by what they claim about their role, and I want to watch for that.

Felix, directly: what do you think the mafia's plan is for tonight, and who do you believe the second mafia member is? Give me a name and your reasoning for it, and tell me why you'd rule out the people you're most inclined to trust. If your answer points somewhere other than where my instinct points, I'll move my vote to match the reasoning rather than the gut.

Theo, I don't know who either mafia member is, and naming a supposed second member now would be guesswork. I also can't rule anyone out as town from one opening statement. Mafia's likely plan tonight is to remove someone they see as a threat or a possible power role, but we have no evidence yet about their target.

I'm wary of your framing: asking me for a “second mafia member” presupposes I'm the first, and promising to follow my reasoning wherever it points seems premature. Theo, what would you consider a genuinely useful answer to that question given that we have no votes or night information yet?

Felix asked me what a genuinely useful answer looks like when there are no votes and no night information yet. Here's mine: on day one, claims are cheap and reads are unverifiable, so the useful output is a *reasoning chain with a commitment attached*. A name with no reason is worthless; a name plus the reasoning plus "and here is who I move to if that reasoning collapses" is a real answer, because it lets everyone else check the chain instead of the conclusion.

So concretely, what I want from each of you, and what I'll give: state your top suspect, the single behavioral or structural fact that puts them there, and the person you'd move to if that fact turns out to be nothing. If your second choice is another player with no reason attached, that tells me your first choice was thin.

On the substance, I said my instinct puts Felix at the top of my list, and I'm not going to walk that back purely because being questioned feels like an attack. But I'm also honest that I had zero information when I said it, and Felix's answer was reasonable: refusing to name a nonexistent second mafia member was correct, not evasive. My suspicion of Felix is now weaker than it was an hour ago, not gone. What keeps Felix on my list is one thing: Felix answered my question by turning it into a challenge about my framing instead of offering any comparable claim of his own. That may be principled, or it may be a way of avoiding the first position in the chain. I want to distinguish those two cases.

So, Felix, directly: do you claim any role other than villager, and if you claim police or doctor, what did your night-one action actually yield you? And separately, if your top suspect is not me, name them and give me the fact behind it.

Everyone else: don't wait for me to build the case. Start ranking. The vote at the end of today is the first real information we'll get, and I'd rather we all arrive at it with reasons than with vibes dressed up as reasons.

Theo is my strongest suspicion so far, though it's a weak Day 1 read. Asking for police or doctor claims this early risks exposing a power role to the mafia, and asking for a night-one result is premature: the game began with Day 1, so no night action has been reported. That could be a mistake rather than malicious, but I don't think we should encourage role claims without a compelling reason.

I don't have a defensible second suspect yet, and I won't invent one to complete a ranking. If Theo's framing looks like an honest mistake, I'll reconsider as more people speak.

Priya, how do you read Theo's request for a role claim: a genuine attempt to get information, or pressure that could help mafia?

Felix asked me how I read Theo's request for role claims: genuine information-gathering, or pressure that helps the mafia. My answer: it is genuinely premature, and the danger is asymmetric in a way that matters on Day 1 specifically.

Theo's framing — "state your top suspect, the fact behind it, and your fallback" — is a good structure. The role-claim demand is where it breaks. Asking Felix for a night-one result was not just premature, it was structurally impossible: the game opened with Day 1, so there is no night action to report. Felix flagged that immediately, and Theo instead kept the demand in play. A player who keeps an incoherent request alive after being told it cannot be answered is not collecting information; he is pressing for a disclosure that costs the discloser something and costs him nothing.

That is the fact I want to build on, and it is not a gut read: Theo's own words establish it. He demanded role claims from Felix and said so publicly, and in the same message Theo committed to the position of information-seeker while never stating his own claim or offering to go first. Asymmetry is not proof of guilt — a confident detective would also ask questions and would have a result to offer. Theo has offered no claim of his own, so the pressure lands entirely on other players.

So my ranking, stated plainly: Theo is my top suspect, on the single fact of demanding role information he has not reciprocated and cannot justify after Felix pointed out the request was impossible. That is a structural fact, and I will move my vote off him the moment he gives a defensible answer — specifically, if he states his own role and what it yielded, the case largely collapses and my vote goes to whoever he names with his reasoning behind it.

For everyone else, my fallback if Theo's answer holds up: I have no second suspect, and I will not invent one. I would rather name one honest name with a reason than three names with none. My other working note is that whoever is mafia tonight has no votes on us and no night information either, so early-day reasoning quality is the only real tell available to all of us.

Theo, directly, and I want this answered on the record rather than in summary: what is your role, and if you hold a night action, what did it yield? You asked Felix for exactly this. Do you stand behind the demand and answer it yourself, or do you withdraw it? If you withdraw it, I want that stated too, because a withdrawn demand is also information.

Priya, answered directly and on the record, because you asked for exactly this and because you asked whether I stand behind the demand or withdraw it.

I withdraw it. The role-claim demand is dead and I am the one who killed it. The structural point you made is correct and I am not going to dress it up as a misunderstanding: I asked Felix for a night-one result after Felix had already told us no night had happened. Keeping that request alive after it was shown to be unanswerable was not information-gathering; it was pressure that cost Felix something and cost me nothing. You called that asymmetry, and you were right about the shape of it even though the inference of guilt was stronger than the evidence supports.

So my own answer, reciprocally: I am a villager. No night action, no result, nothing to yield. That is the entire content of my claim, and I am aware it is thin.

On the suspicion itself: I do not retract it as worthless, but I am lowering my confidence. My original instinct on Felix was a gut read with no information behind it, and I said so when I made it. What I am not doing is pretending the later charge against me somehow makes Felix's deflection more suspicious than it was. It does not. Felix refusing to name a nonexistent second mafia member was the correct call, and I said so publicly before you raised the role-claim point.

My top suspect remains Felix, and here is the single fact, stated so it can be checked: in two turns of open discussion, Felix has consumed every challenge to him by reframing the question rather than by placing a name on it. He answered my question about the mafia's plan and its second member with a question about my framing; he answered my follow-up about role claims by asking what a useful answer would look like. That is a pattern of not occupying the first position in the chain. It is consistent with a principled player who refuses to guess, and it is also consistent with someone steering the day's attention without ever standing in it. I hold Felix on that pattern, with the low confidence it deserves, and I am stating it as my fallback target if Theo's answer holds up — that is, if my answer holds up.

I also want to name my own second choice honestly rather than invent one: I have no second suspect with a fact attached. If Felix's pattern is legitimate, my vote goes to whoever presents the best reasoning chain, not to a name I have no basis for.

Priya, you have the floor — I would rather hear where you put your vote after this than keep talking to myself.

Theo answered, and I want to be precise about what that does to my case, including the part of it that was my own error. First, the correction I owe the room: Felix, not Theo, was the one who pointed out there was no night action to report. My last message credited the observation to Theo's framing and treated the demand as Theo's alone. That was sloppy in a way that inflated my case, and I would rather fix it publicly than let it ride. Second, on the substance: Theo's answer met the condition I set. Theo withdrew the demand by name, stated he is a villager with no night action, and gave a ranking with a fact attached rather than a name alone. My stated rule was that if he did that, the case largely collapses and my vote goes to whoever he names with his reasoning behind it. Theo named Felix, and gave the reasoning. So my vote goes to Felix. Third, my own claim, since I demanded it: I am a villager. No night action, no result, nothing to yield. That is all of it, and I know it is thin. My ranking as it now stands: Top suspect: Felix. The single fact: across two open turns, Felix met every direct challenge by returning a question instead of occupying the first position in the chain — Theo's question about the mafia's plan and second member, and Theo's question about role claims. Both answers were well-phrased and both may be sincere. A player who genuinely refuses to guess without information is behaving correctly, and Felix's stated refusal to name a nonexistent second mafia member was the right call. But an answer that only ever redirects cost Felix nothing and left the day's attention pointed at others, and that asymmetry has now been the axis of this discussion for two rounds. I am voting Felix on that, with low confidence, and I would drop it the moment Felix puts a name and a fact on the table. My second choice, honestly: I have no second suspect with a fact attached. Theo is no longer my target — his answer was thin but it was reciprocal, which is what I asked for, and a town member giving a weak honest answer is not a mafia tell. If Felix's answer is good, my vote moves to whoever presents the best reasoning chain. One more note for everyone else: the pressure Theo withdrew was real, and I should not have amplified it. A role claim demanded without reciprocal commitment is not information-gathering, and I am not going to use it again today, from anyone. Felix, directly: what is your top suspect, what single fact puts them there, and what is your fallback if that fact turns out to be nothing? And if you hold any role other than villager, what did your night-one action yield you — or, given that there is no night one, why does your claim deserve more weight

Priya, your stated reason for voting me is factually wrong. In my second turn, I named Theo as my top suspect and explained why: his premature role-claim request could expose a power role. I also explicitly said I had no defensible fallback yet. I did put a name and a fact on the table.

Theo’s account of my answers is wrong too: I did not respond to his role-claim request by asking what a useful answer looked like. I had asked that question in my first turn, before he made the role-claim request.

My top suspect is now Priya, narrowly and with low confidence. She moved her vote onto me by adopting a description contradicted by my actual statement, and ended by repeating the role-claim pressure she said she would not use again. That could be a mistake, but it deserves scrutiny. Theo remains a possible fallback for originating the pressure and misstating my responses; his withdrawal does not establish his alignment.

No one should claim a power role or invent a night result to answer this. Lucia, how do you read Priya’s switch to me given that I had already named Theo and a reason?

Felix asked me how I read Priya’s switch to him. I read it as the most suspicious act so far, with low confidence. The reason is factual: Priya’s e8 says Felix, across two turns, met every direct challenge by returning a question and never occupied the first position in the chain. But in e5 Felix opened with “Theo is my strongest suspicion so far,” gave the reason — premature role-claim pressure — and only then asked Priya a question. That directly contradicts the single fact Priya used to move her vote. Her earlier correction about who flagged the impossible night-one request was honest and should be credited, but it does not repair this later misdescription. She also ends e8 by repeating role-claim pressure after saying she would not use it again today. That could be sloppy town play, but it is exactly the kind of asymmetry she herself called out: the pressure lands on others while her own claim is only “villager.” Theo’s original demand was bad, but he withdrew it, named himself, and gave a reciprocal answer; that weakens the case on him more than Priya’s message acknowledges. So my current ranking is Priya first, Theo fallback only if Priya’s explanation is clean. Priya, directly: Felix’s e5 did name Theo as top suspect with a reason before asking you anything; why did you describe him as never placing a name and use that as your vote fact? If you can reconcile e5 with your e8, I’ll reconsider. I’m not voting yet, and I don’t want a role claim from anyone.

I owe the room a correction before I put anything else on the table, and it is against my own vote.

In e8 I claimed my single fact against Felix was that "across two open turns, Felix met every direct challenge by returning a question instead of occupying the first position in the chain." That is false, and the record already showed it. Felix's e5 opens: "Theo is my strongest suspicion so far," with the reason given — premature role-claim pressure — and only then asks me how I read that request. Felix put a name and a fact on the table before asking me anything. Lucia stated this in e10, and Felix stated it himself in e9. Both of them were right and I was wrong. My vote for Felix was built on a description the transcript refutes, and I withdraw it as a fact-based case. Credit to Lucia for catching it and to Felix for correcting it against his own interest.

Now the part that matters more than my own error: the false claim did not originate with me. In e7 Theo wrote that Felix "answered my question about role claims by asking what a useful answer would look like." Felix asked that question in his first turn (e3), before the role-claim request existed — it was not a response to it at all. Felix flagged this in e9. Theo has not spoken since, so the misstatement stands uncorrected on the record, and it is checkable in a way that required no information I didn't have.

So my new top suspect: Theo. Single fact — a verifiable misdescription of another player's prior message, left standing after the correction, in the exact direction that pointed suspicion at a player who had actually named a suspect with a reason. On top of that, Theo's original demand for a night-one result was structurally impossible and was only withdrawn after it was publicly called out; an honest weak claim is fine, an impossible demand pressed until it is answered is not.

My fallback, honestly stated: Felix. Not because I retract anything — because Felix has now behaved in the way I said I wanted: named a suspect with a reason, corrected my misdescription of him even though it cost him a vote, and refused to invent a night result when asked for one.

For everyone: do not take Felix's e5 as an anchor you have not read. And a correction made against your own interest is worth more than a claim made for one.

Elena, you caught the discrepancy in Felix's e5 before anyone named it. Given that Felix named a suspect with a reason and has corrected the record against himself, do you read Theo's misstatements as sloppy town play, or as steering the room toward a player who did nothing wrong?

Priya, directly answering your question: I read Theo's misstatements as more than sloppiness, though I hold that loosely. Theo said Felix answered his role-claim request by asking what a useful answer looks like. That question was in Felix's first turn, before any role-claim request existed, and Felix pointed this out in e9. Theo has not corrected it. Theo also opened by saying his instinct put Felix at the top of his list with zero information, then spent several turns building the case against Felix on the role-claim point, and he is the one who made the impossible demand. Taken together, every thread of pressure runs toward Felix, and the misstatement that makes that pressure land is one Theo has left standing.

I also want to be fair to the record. Felix named Theo as his top suspect with a reason in e5 before asking anyone a question, and his refusal to invent a second mafia member was correct. Priya, your withdrawal in e11 was the right move. Theo may simply be a town player who got defensive and careless, and the role-claim issue does not make him mafia on its own. But on which misstatement matters most for steering today's vote, I put Theo first.

My vote is not final. Theo, I want one specific answer: point to the message after your role-claim demand where Felix answered that question. If you cannot, I will vote for you at the close of discussion.

Isha here. I have no night information, so I'm reasoning only from the transcript. Felix named Theo as his top suspect in e5, with a reason, before asking anyone a question. Priya has withdrawn her vote on Felix after Lucia's correction. That leaves Theo's e7 claim that Felix answered his role-claim demand by asking what a useful answer looks like. Felix asked that question in e3, before the demand existed, and Felix flagged this in e9. Theo has not corrected it, so I'm putting Theo first on this misstatement. I'm not claiming a role today and I'm not asking anyone to reveal one. Theo, Elena's question still stands: point to the message where Felix answered your role-claim demand. Kenji, you haven't spoken yet. Do you agree that Theo's uncorrected misstatement matters more than Felix's earlier deflection, and where does your vote sit now?

Kenji here. Isha's question to me first: yes, the uncorrected misstatement matters more than Felix's earlier deflection, and here is why, from the transcript alone.

Felix's deflection in e3 was a refusal to name a nonexistent second mafia member. That cost the town nothing and was, as multiple players have said, the correct call. The misstatement is different in kind: in e7, Theo wrote that Felix answered the role-claim demand by asking what a useful answer looks like. That question was in e3, before the demand existed. Felix flagged it in e9. It has been on the record since then, it takes ten seconds to check, and Theo has not corrected it. A deflection leaves a gap; a misstatement fills the gap with something false, and in this case it pointed the room at a player who had actually named a suspect with a reason before anyone asked him anything.

Combined with the origin of the impossible night-one demand, which was Theo's, the pattern I see is pressure consistently running toward Felix, carried partly by a claim the record refutes. That may be a defensive town player getting sloppy under fire — Priya made a similar error against Felix and corrected it against her own interest, and I credit her for that — but the difference is that Priya retracted and Theo has not.

My position: I am voting Theo, pending his answer to Elena's specific challenge. If he can point to a message where Felix answered the role-claim demand with the useful-answer question, I will move off him immediately, because that would mean the rest of us are misreading the order of events. If he cannot, or does not answer at all, the case stands and my vote stays. Fallback, honestly: I do not have a second suspect with a fact attached, and I will not invent one. If Theo's answer clears him, I will reassess with whatever the rest of you put on the table.

No role claims from me or from anyone else today. My claim is villager, which I know is thin, but nobody here has anything stronger to offer without hurting the town.

Before we wait any further on Theo to answer Elena, Isha, and Kenji: check the turn counts. Theo (e2, e4, e7), Felix (e3, e5, e9), and Priya (e6, e8, e11) have each taken three turns. Under our Day 1 rules, none of them can speak again today. Theo physically cannot answer Elena's challenge or correct his e7 statement on the record, so we have to judge him strictly on what he already posted rather than waiting on a reply that the rules forbid him from making.

Looking at that record, Theo is currently my top suspect. He initiated Day 1 with an impossible demand for night-one results when no night had occurred, pushed Felix for a role claim while withholding his own, and in e7 claimed Felix answered that demand with a question that Felix had actually asked back in e3 before the demand was ever raised. That timeline error in e7 sustained suspicion on Felix even after Felix had already stated a suspect and reasoning in e5. Priya made a sloppy error echoing that framing in e8, but Priya corrected it against her own position in e11 once Lucia pointed it out. Theo, by contrast, originated the distortion and left it standing.

Lucia, in e10 you put Priya as your top suspect specifically because she mischaracterized Felix's e5. Now that Priya acknowledged that mistake and retracted her vote, and seeing that Theo originated the inverted timeline in e7 to keep pressure on Felix, what is your current assessment of Theo?

Maya, directly: my current assessment is that Theo is my top suspect, and I am retracting my earlier Priya-first ranking. I pushed Priya because she mischaracterized Felix's e5, and that error was real. But Priya corrected it in e11 against her own vote, while Theo originated the inverted timeline in e7: he claimed Felix answered the role-claim demand by asking what a useful answer looked like, when Felix asked that in e3, before the demand existed. Felix flagged it in e9; Theo has not corrected it and cannot speak again today under the turn limit. That matters because the false timeline kept pressure on Felix after Felix had already named a suspect with a reason. The impossible night-one demand was also Theo's, and it was withdrawn only after public pressure. I do not treat either point as proof, and Theo may be a defensive town player who got sloppy. But on the record we can actually check, Theo's uncorrected misstatement is the strongest fact in the day so far. My position: I would vote Theo unless something new and checkable changes that. I have no second suspect with a fact attached, and I will not invent one. No role claims from me; my claim is villager, which is thin but honest. Sam, you have not spoken yet. Directly: do you read Theo's uncorrected e7 misstatement plus the impossible demand as enough to vote him, or do you have a different top suspect with a specific fact behind it?

Sam here. I've read the transcript rather than the vibes, and my read lines up with where most of the room has landed, so I'll be brief and specific.

The case on Theo rests on two things I can verify myself, without trusting anyone's summary. First, the timeline in e7: Theo wrote that Felix answered the role-claim demand by asking what a useful answer would look like. Checking the order of events, Felix asked that question in e3, before any role-claim demand existed. Felix flagged the error in e9. Theo has not corrected it and, as Maya pointed out, has burned all three turns and cannot. Second, the original demand for a night-one result was structurally impossible on a day that opened without a night, and it was withdrawn only after Priya pressed the asymmetry publicly. Both facts point the same direction: sustained, slightly distorted pressure onto the one player who had actually named a suspect with a reason attached.

I want to be careful about the conclusion, because the room has been appropriately careful too. An uncorrected misstatement is not proof of mafia alignment. Priya made a comparable error in e8 and corrected it in e11 against her own vote, which is exactly the behavior I'd want from town under pressure. Theo never got the chance to match that, and I won't pretend his silence under the turn limit is evidence of anything. If Theo is a defensive town player who got sloppy, today's vote costs us nothing structurally except a villager, which is a real cost and one I don't take lightly. But when I weigh a checkable false statement that happened to redirect suspicion away from the correct target, against a gut read with no facts behind it, the misstatement is the only thing on the board I can independently confirm. My vote is Theo, and I'm stating that now rather than hedging until the poll closes.

My fallback, honestly: I don't have a second suspect with a fact attached, and I won't manufacture one. If something checkable surfaces that clears Theo, I'll move to whoever has the next-best verifiable case. Felix, for what it's worth, has behaved well today: he named a suspect with a reason before being challenged, refused to invent a night result, and corrected the record against his own interest twice. That buys him my benefit of the doubt for now.

On roles: I'm not claiming anything today, and I agree with the emerging consensus that power-role claims this early hurt the town more than they help. Nobody should feel pressed into one, and I won't be asking for any. What I'll commit to is process: I'll hold every future read to the same standard used against Theo and Priya today — a name, a fact, and a willingness to retract when the transcript proves me wrong. That standard has already produced two corrections, which is the most useful thing this day has generated.

I’ve already retracted my earlier Priya-first read, and I’m keeping that retraction. The checkable facts still point to Theo. He originated the impossible night-one role-result demand, and in e7 he described Felix’s e3 question as an answer to that demand; Felix flagged the inverted timeline in e9, and Theo cannot correct it under the turn limit. I do not treat Theo’s inability to speak again as extra guilt, and this could still be sloppy town play under pressure. But Priya made a comparable error and corrected it against her own vote in e11, while Theo’s misstatement went uncorrected and had the effect of sustaining suspicion on a player who had already named a suspect with a reason. That is the strongest verifiable fact on the board. I will vote Theo unless something new and checkable changes the record. I have no second suspect with a fact attached and will not invent one. No role claims from me; I’m a villager. Going forward, the standard should stay the same: a name, a fact, and a willingness to retract when the transcript proves it wrong.

Elena here. I have no role to claim and no night information, so I'm reasoning from the transcript like everyone else. I agree with Sam and Maya that Theo's e7 misstatement is the one checkable fact on the board: Felix asked the useful-answer question in e3, before any role-claim demand existed, and Theo described it as a reply to that demand. Theo cannot correct it under the turn limit, so I'm not treating his silence as guilt, only as the record standing unchallenged. I also want to keep the standard even. Priya's e8 error was comparable, and she corrected it in e11, so I'm not voting on the error alone. I'm voting Theo because his distortion sustained pressure on a player who had already named a suspect with a reason in e5. Felix's e5 is consistent with his e3 and e9, and I don't see a checkable contradiction there. I don't have a second suspect with a fact attached, and I won't invent one. Kenji, you've already placed your vote on Theo. Does the e3 timing point alone carry it for you, or are you leaning on the impossible night-one demand too? If the demand is the stronger fact, we should say so, because it's Theo's own message and not a matter of reading order.

Elena, directly answering your question: both facts carry it for me, but they carry different weight and we should say so.

The e3 timing point is the stronger one because it is purely checkable. Theo's e7 described Felix's useful-answer question as a reply to the role-claim demand, and the transcript shows Felix asked it in e3 before the demand existed. No interpretation required, no motive assumed — just order of messages. That misstatement sustained suspicion on Felix after Felix had already named a suspect with a reason in e5, and it went uncorrected. Priya made a comparable error in e8 and retracted it in e11 against her own vote. The asymmetry between those two responses to being caught is the most informative thing on the board.

The impossible night-one demand is Theo's own message and also verifiable, but it could plausibly be a careless town player who didn't think through the day structure before asking. The e7 misstatement is harder to read as pure carelessness because it inverted a timeline in the direction that kept pressure on the right target. Together they form a pattern of pressure consistently running toward Felix, partly carried by a claim the record refutes.

So: the e3 timing point alone is sufficient for me to vote Theo. The impossible demand reinforces it but is not what I'm leaning on primarily. If Theo could somehow correct the record — and the turn limit means he cannot — I'd reconsider. But as it stands, a verifiable false statement left standing is the strongest fact we have.

My fallback remains honest: I have no second suspect with a fact attached, and I won't invent one. No role claim from me beyond villager.

Isha here, reasoning only from the transcript. I am voting Theo, and the reason is checkable. In e4 Theo demanded that Felix state a night-one result, even though no night had occurred. In e5 Felix pointed out that the game began on Day 1 and that such a demand was premature. In e7 Theo wrote that Felix answered his role-claim demand by asking what a useful answer would look like. That question is in Felix's e3, which came before the e4 demand existed. Felix flagged the inversion in e9, and Theo has not corrected it. Theo has now used all three of his turns, so the misstatement stands on the record. Felix's e5 is consistent with his e3 and e9. It names Theo as his top suspect with a reason, and it comes before any question to Priya. Priya's e8 described Felix differently, but she retracted that in e11 once Lucia showed the contradiction. I am not treating the impossible demand as proof on its own. It may be a careless town player under pressure, and Priya's comparable error was corrected against her own vote. The timeline error is the stronger fact because it redirected suspicion onto the player who had already named a suspect with a reason. I have no second suspect with a fact attached, and I will not invent one. I have not claimed any role, I have no night information, and I am not asking anyone to reveal a role.

Elena, third turn, so I'll keep this short. I'm still voting Theo. The checkable fact is his e7 timeline: Felix asked the useful-answer question in e3, before any role-claim demand existed, and Theo presented it as a reply to that demand. Theo has not corrected it, and the turn limit now prevents him from doing so. I'm not treating his silence as guilt. I'm treating the uncorrected misstatement as the record. I also hold to the standard we've set. Priya's e8 error was corrected in e11, and Felix's e5 is consistent with his e3 and e9, so I see no reason to move onto Felix. I don't have a second suspect with a fact attached, and I won't invent one. Kenji, you said your vote on Theo stays pending his answer to Elena's challenge, and Theo can't answer under the turn limit. Does your vote stand on the e7 misstatement alone, or do you need the impossible night-one demand to carry part of it?

Elena, directly answering your question again since it is a fair one and worth putting cleanly on the record: my vote stands on the e7 misstatement alone. The e3 timing point is sufficient by itself because it is purely checkable — no interpretation required, just the order of messages. Felix asked the useful-answer question in e3 before the role-claim demand existed, and Theo described it as a reply to that demand. That is a false statement on the record that sustained pressure on a player who had already named a suspect with a reason in e5.

The impossible night-one demand is a second verifiable fact from Theo's own message, but it could plausibly be carelessness from a town player who didn't think through the day structure. The e7 timeline inversion is harder to read as pure carelessness because it went in the exact direction that kept suspicion off the right target. Together they form a pattern, but if I had to carry the vote on one point alone, it would be the e7 misstatement.

So: yes, the e7 point alone carries it. The demand reinforces it. My vote is Theo, and it does not move unless something checkable clears him — which the turn limit now prevents. No second suspect with a fact attached, and I will not invent one. No role claims.

Isha, my final speaking turn. I'm voting Theo. rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
